title: CoAP Explained: Constrained Application Protocol — Full Exam Revision
description: A complete animated revision of CoAP, the Constrained Application Protocol: constrained networks, devices and resources, CoAP vs HTTP, the message format, codes and message IDs, methods, URIs, CON / NON / ACK / RST messaging, piggybacked and separate responses, retransmission with exponential back-off, OBSERVE and block transfer.

pronounce.coap://example.com:5683/~sensors/temp.xm: co-app, colon, slash slash, example dot com, colon five six eight three, slash tilde sensors, slash temp dot X M L

scenes.title: What is CoAP?
lines: How does a tiny battery-powered sensor talk to the internet, when it is too weak to run normal web protocols?
The answer is CoAP, the Constrained Application Protocol.
CoAP is defined by the IETF CoRE working group. CoRE stands for Constrained RESTful Environments.
Its job is the manipulation of resources on a device that sits on a constrained IP network.
In this revision we cover every slide: from constrained networks, through the message format, to OBSERVE and block transfer.

scenes.title: What CoAP is, and is not
lines: First, what CoAP is.
CoAP is a RESTful protocol.
It supports both synchronous and asynchronous communication.
It is built for constrained devices and constrained networks.
It is specialized for M2M, machine to machine, applications.
And it is easy to proxy to and from HTTP.
Now, what CoAP is not.
It is not a replacement for HTTP.
It is not a general HTTP compression scheme.
And it is not separate from the web. It fits into the web through proxies.

scenes.title: Constrained IP networks
lines: So what is a constrained IP network?
It has limited packet sizes.
It may show a high degree of packet loss.
And it may have many devices that are powered off most of the time, but periodically wake up for brief periods.
These networks and their nodes have severe limits on throughput, on available power,
and on complexity, because each node has limited code size and limited RAM.
Low-Power Wireless Personal Area Networks, called LoWPANs, are an example of this type of network.
Constrained networks appear in home and building automation, energy management, and the Internet of Things.

scenes.title: Devices and resources
lines: The general architecture is made of nodes on the constrained network, called Devices.
Each Device is responsible for one or more Resources.
A resource may represent a sensor, an actuator, a combination of values, or other information.
Devices send messages to change and to query resources on other Devices.
Devices can send notifications about changed resource values to Devices that have subscribed to them.
And a Device can also publish its resources, or be queried about them.

scenes.title: Application scope
lines: CoAP targets the operating environments defined by the ROLL and 6LoWPAN working groups.
These have extra constraints compared to normal IP networks.
But CoAP also operates over traditional IP networks.
Applications include monitoring simple sensors, like temperature sensors, light switches, and power meters.
Controlling actuators, like light switches, heating controllers, and door locks.
And managing devices.

scenes.title: CoAP vs HTTP and the CoAP layers
lines: Like HTTP, CoAP is a way of structuring REST communications, but it is optimized for M2M applications.
TCP and HTTP are considered too heavy for 6LoWPAN devices such as sensors.
So CoAP is based on UDP, with a compressed and simplified message exchange.
Here is the CoAP RESTful application stack.
At the bottom is UDP.
Above it, CoAP is split into two sub-layers. The messages layer handles reliability and duplicates.
The request and response layer carries the REST methods and response codes.
And the application sits on top.

scenes.title: CoAP message format
lines: Now the CoAP message format. It starts with a fixed four byte header.
Ver is the version, two bits, and it is set to one.
T is the message type, two bits.
Zero is CON, confirmable. One is NON, non-confirmable. Two is ACK, acknowledgement. Three is RST, reset.
TKL is the token length, four bits.
Code is eight bits: a three bit class and a five bit detail, written as c.dd.
The class says request, zero; success response, two; client error, four; or server error, five.
Message ID is sixteen bits, an identifier used to match responses.
After the header comes the Token, TKL bytes long, used to correlate requests and responses.
Then any Options.
Then a marker byte of eight ones, 0xFF, and finally the payload, if any.

scenes.title: Code and Message ID
lines: The Code compresses the three digit HTTP text representation into one byte.
For requests, the first three bits are zero zero zero.
The next five bits pick the method: one is GET, two is POST, three is PUT, four is DELETE.
For responses, the first three bits hold the first digit of the HTTP code: two for success, four for client error, five for server error.
The next five bits hold the last two digits.
So HTTP 201 becomes zero one zero, then zero zero zero zero one. That is 2.01.
And HTTP 400 becomes one zero zero, then all zeros. That is 4.00.
You will also see 2.05, which means Content, a successful response carrying data.
The Message ID is used in the acknowledgement process, to tie a request with its response.

scenes.title: CoAP methods
lines: CoAP uses GET, PUT, POST and DELETE, in a similar manner to HTTP.
GET reads a resource, POST creates or processes, PUT updates, and DELETE removes it.
But new methods can be added, and they do not necessarily have to use requests and responses in pairs.
For example, OBSERVE. One request can produce many responses over time.

scenes.title: CoAP URI
lines: A CoAP URI looks a lot like a web address.
It is coap, colon, slash slash, then the host, an optional port, a path, and an optional query.
For example, coap://example.com:5683/~sensors/temp.xml.
Port 5683 is the default CoAP port.
This second form, with the host in capitals and the tilde written as %7E, points to the same resource.
The secure version uses the scheme coaps, with exactly the same structure. It runs over DTLS, on port 5684.

scenes.title: Reliable messages: CON and ACK
lines: CoAP has two messaging modes. First, reliable message transmission.
Reliability is provided by marking a message as Confirmable, CON.
Here the client sends CON with Message ID 0x7d34.
The server replies with an ACK carrying the same Message ID, 0x7d34.
If no ACK arrives, the confirmable message is retransmitted using a default timeout,
with exponential back-off between retransmissions, until the recipient sends an acknowledgement.

scenes.title: Unreliable messages: NON
lines: Second, unreliable message transmission.
A message that does not need reliable delivery can be sent as Non-confirmable, NON.
Here the client sends NON with Message ID 0x01a0.
NON messages are not acknowledged. No ACK comes back, and nothing is retransmitted.
This suits frequent sensor readings, where a lost value is soon replaced by the next one.

scenes.title: Example 1: synchronous exchange
lines: Example one: a synchronous message exchange.
The client sends a CONfirmable message, MID 0x1234, and starts a timer.
The server sends an ACK with the same MID, 0x1234, and the response is piggybacked inside that ACK. The timer stops.
Next, the client sends CON, MID 0x1235.
But this time the ACK is lost on the way back.
The client's timer expires, so it resends the message, with the same MID 0x1235.
Now the ACK arrives, and the timer stops.
Between retransmissions, the waiting time grows with exponential back-off. Each timeout is roughly double the last one.

scenes.title: Example 2a: asynchronous, separate response
lines: Example two a: an asynchronous message exchange.
The client sends CON, MID 0x7a10, GET /temperature, with token 0x73.
The server cannot answer yet, so it immediately sends an empty ACK, with MID 0x7a10. This stops the client retransmitting.
Time passes.
When the response is ready, the server sends it in a new CON message, with a new MID 0x23bb.
It carries 2.05 Content, the same token 0x73, and the payload, twenty two point five degrees C.
The client acknowledges with ACK 0x23bb.
Key point: the token links request and response. The Message ID only links each message to its ACK.

scenes.title: Example 2b: asynchronous with NON
lines: Example two b: asynchronous, with non-confirmable messages.
The client sends NON, MID 0x7a11, GET /temperature, with token 0x74.
The response is sent using a new Non-confirmable message, MID 0x23bc, 2.05 Content, token 0x74, twenty two point five C.
No acknowledgements anywhere.
The server may instead send the response as a Confirmable message, if it wants an acknowledgement.

scenes.title: Example 3a: OBSERVE
lines: Example three a: OBSERVE, periodic responses from a server.
The client sends a CONfirmable message, MID 0x1234, token 0x22, with the OBSERVE option set to zero, asking for periodic responses.
The server acknowledges with ACK, MID 0x1234, and the client's timer stops.
Now the server sends NON responses, all with the same token, 0x22.
The first is MID 0xABCD, with OBSERVE equal to ten.
The OBSERVE number in each response increases, to indicate the order of the responses.
Here, OBSERVE twenty is delayed in the network, and arrives after OBSERVE thirty.
So the client ignores OBSERVE twenty, because it is older than the thirty it already has.
Either the client or the server can terminate the observation.

scenes.title: Example 3b: OBSERVE notifications
lines: Example three b shows the same idea with real values.
Registration: the client sends GET /temperature, token 0x4a, observe zero.
The server replies with a notification of the current state: 2.05 Content, observe twelve, twenty two point nine Celsius.
When the state changes, it notifies again: observe forty four, twenty two point eight.
And again: observe sixty, twenty three point one. Every notification carries the same token, 0x4a.
A notification can be confirmable or non-confirmable.
The server may send a confirmable notification to request an acknowledgement from the client.

scenes.title: Example 4: block transfer
lines: Example four: block transfer from server to client.
The resource /light is four thousand ninety six bytes, too big for one small packet. So it is split into four blocks of one thousand twenty four bytes.
First, the client sends a CONfirmable GET /light.
The server replies ACK, block number zero, more flag one, size one thousand twenty four, with 2.05. The more flag says it has more blocks to send.
The client then asks for more: CON, block number one, GET /light. The server returns block one, more equals one.
Then block two, again with more equals one.
Finally block three, with more equals zero. That was the last block.
The block option value has three fields. NUM is the block number. M is the more flag.
And SZX encodes the block size. Size equals two to the power of SZX plus four, so SZX six means one thousand twenty four.

scenes.title: Summary
lines: To summarise the slides.
CoAP is applicable to any IP network, not only constrained ones.
Open source software is available for these protocols.
For example, CoAPy, the Constrained Application Protocol in Python, at coapy dot sourceforge dot net.

scenes.title: Exam recap
lines: Quick exam recap.
CoAP: by IETF CoRE, RESTful, over UDP, for constrained M2M devices.
Header: version two bits, type two bits, token length four bits, code eight bits, message ID sixteen bits.
Types: CON zero, NON one, ACK two, RST three.
Code is c.dd: zero for requests, two success, four client error, five server error.
Message ID matches a message to its ACK. Token matches a request to its response.
CON is retransmitted with exponential back-off. NON is never acknowledged.
Piggybacked responses ride inside the ACK. Separate responses come later in a new message.
OBSERVE gives ordered notifications, and older ones are ignored. Block transfer splits big resources with NUM, M and SZX.
Good luck in your exam!
